relationship: Midianite oppression and its subsequent reversal
rationale: Israel is delivered into Midian's hand for seven years; the later notice records Midian humbled and forty years of quiet in Gideon's days.

relationship: Same-chapter oppressive circumstances and concealed food preparation
rationale: Israel makes mountain enclosures, caves and strongholds because of Midian; Gideon's wheat-beating in a winepress likewise occurs to escape Midian.

relationship: Same-chapter named raiding coalition and its military assembly
rationale: Midian, Amalek and the sons of the east attack Israel's sowing; the same three named groups later gather and camp in Jezreel's valley.

relationship: Same-chapter destruction of livelihood and resulting impoverishment
rationale: The raiders destroy produce and leave neither flock, calf nor donkey; Israel's subsequent poverty and cry to the Lord describe the oppression's effect.

relationship: Repeated locust comparison and innumerable camels
rationale: Both camp descriptions compare the invaders' multitude to locusts and call their camels beyond numbering; the later account also compares them to seashore sand.

relationship: Same-chapter cry under Midian and the prophetic response
rationale: Israel's poverty prompts a cry to the Lord; the following account answers that cry with a prophet recalling rescue from Egypt and Israel's disobedience.

relationship: Same-chapter appeal to the Lord and the message sent in answer
rationale: The cry because of Midian introduces the Lord's sending a prophet, whose message contrasts His former rescue with the people's failure to obey.

relationship: Shared divine self-identification as the deliverer from slavery
rationale: Both identify the Lord as the One who brought Israel out of Egypt and the house of slavery; Judges places that declaration in the prophet's rebuke.

relationship: Divine rescue from opponents and gift of their land
rationale: The prophet recalls rescue and dispossession of Israel's oppressors; Joshua's recital specifically narrates victory over the eastern Amorites and inheritance of their land.

relationship: Exclusive allegiance amid the Amorites' gods
rationale: Judges recalls the prohibition on fearing the Amorites' gods and charges disobedience; Joshua presents service of those gods as an alternative to his household's service of the Lord.

relationship: Same-chapter Gideon's concealment within the oppression account
rationale: Gideon beats wheat in a winepress to escape Midian, giving a particular instance alongside Israel's mountain enclosures, caves and strongholds made because of Midian.

relationship: Divine presence assured to an appointed deliverer
rationale: The messenger greets Gideon with the Lord's presence; God likewise promises to be with Moses in his commissioned task of bringing Israel out of Egypt.

relationship: Same-chapter disputed exodus memory and the prophet's explanation
rationale: Gideon asks why remembered exodus wonders coexist with Midian's power; the prophet has already recalled the same rescue and accused Israel of not obeying.

relationship: Exodus deliverance behind Gideon's remembered wonders
rationale: Gideon appeals to the fathers' account that the Lord brought Israel from Egypt; Exodus supplies the particular sea deliverance and Israel's recognition of the Lord's great hand.

relationship: Commissioning a deliverer to bring Israel out of oppression
rationale: Gideon is sent to save Israel; Moses is similarly sent to Pharaoh to bring Israel from Egypt, with the two commissions addressing different oppressors.

relationship: An appointed deliverer's objection to his own adequacy
rationale: Gideon objects that his thousand is lowliest and he is small in his household; Moses asks who he is to confront Pharaoh and bring Israel out.

relationship: Promise of divine accompaniment answers an objection
rationale: Gideon's objection is answered by the Lord's promised presence against Midian; Moses' question about his adequacy is likewise answered by God's promise to be with him.

relationship: Signs as confirmation of a divine encounter
rationale: Gideon requests a sign confirming who speaks with him; Moses receives the staff sign so others may believe that the Lord appeared to him, distinguishing the intended audiences.

relationship: Request that the Lord's messenger remain for a prepared offering
rationale: Gideon asks the visitor to stay while he brings a sacrifice; Manoah similarly urges the messenger to stay for a young goat, and is directed to offer to the Lord.

relationship: Young goat prepared in an encounter with the Lord's messenger
rationale: Gideon prepares a young goat with unleavened cakes and broth; Manoah brings a young goat and sacrifice onto a rock to the Lord.

relationship: Same-chapter placement of the offering and the fire response
rationale: The messenger directs meat and loaves to the rock with poured broth; his staff then touches the food and fire from the rock consumes it.

relationship: Miraculous offering fire and the messenger's departure
rationale: Gideon's food is consumed by fire from the rock and the messenger vanishes; Manoah's messenger ascends in the offering flame and does not appear again.

relationship: Recognizing the messenger and fearing death after the encounter
rationale: Gideon recognizes the Lord's messenger and cries out about seeing him face to face; Manoah likewise recognizes the messenger and fears death because they have seen God.

relationship: Assurance against death following a messenger encounter
rationale: The Lord directly tells Gideon not to fear death; Manoah's wife argues that the Lord's acceptance of their offering and revelation shows He did not wish to kill them.

relationship: Same-chapter declared peace and the altar's name
rationale: Gideon names his altar Peace of the Lord immediately after the Lord's declaration of peace and reassurance that he will not die.

relationship: Destruction of rival altars and sacred groves
rationale: Gideon is commanded to pull down his father's Baal altar and cut its grove; Deuteronomy likewise commands destruction of altars and cutting down sacred groves.

relationship: Same-chapter commanded Lord's altar and the reported burnt offering
rationale: The Lord commands a new altar and a bull as whole burnt offering; the morning discovery reports the demolished Baal altar, cut grove and bull offered on the new altar.

relationship: Same-chapter nighttime execution of the altar commands
rationale: Gideon and thirteen servants carry out the instructions concerning the Baal altar, grove and Lord's altar; the narrative specifically says fear led him to act at night.

relationship: Same-chapter morning discovery corresponds to the night's instructions
rationale: What the townsmen find—the demolished Baal altar, cut grove and bull burnt offering on the new altar—corresponds to the Lord's preceding commands.

relationship: Same-chapter discovered responsibility and the narrator's earlier account
rationale: The townsmen's investigation identifies Gideon son of Joash as responsible; the narrator has already described Gideon taking thirteen servants and performing the deed at night.

relationship: Same-chapter demand for Gideon's death and Joash's counterchallenge
rationale: The townsmen demand Gideon's death for demolishing Baal's altar and grove; Joash challenges their defense of Baal and says the supposed god should avenge his own altar.

relationship: Same-chapter conflicting responses to the demolished Baal altar
rationale: The townsmen seek to execute the man who damaged Baal's altar; Joash instead questions why they defend Baal and insists that a god should avenge himself.

relationship: Same-chapter Tribunal of Baal notice and the challenge to Baal's agency
rationale: The name Tribunal of Baal accompanies the demolished altar after Joash has challenged Baal to avenge that same altar.

relationship: Repeated description of the assembled eastern enemy coalition
rationale: Midian, Amalek and the sons of the east gather in Jezreel's valley; the later valley-camp description names those same groups and emphasizes their multitude.

relationship: Divine Spirit equipping Israel's deliverer
rationale: The Spirit clothes Gideon before his trumpet summons; the earlier account names Othniel as deliverer and describes the Lord's Spirit upon him as he judges and goes to war.

relationship: Tribal summons followed by pursuit of Midian
rationale: Manasseh, Asher and Naphtali occur in both the initial summons and later pursuit; Zebulun is also named in the first summons but not in the later list.

relationship: Same-chapter proposed confirmation refers back to the commission
rationale: Gideon's conditional appeal says God has spoken of saving Israel by his hand; the earlier commission sends him to save Israel and promises victory over Midian.

relationship: Same-chapter first fleece condition and its stated result
rationale: Gideon proposes dew on the fleece with dry ground; the next report says it happened and describes squeezing a basin of water from the fleece.

relationship: Same-chapter wet fleece answers the first proposed sign
rationale: The basin of dew squeezed from the fleece is the narrated result of Gideon's preceding request for a wet fleece while the ground remains dry.

relationship: Same-chapter reversed fleece request and its fulfillment
rationale: Gideon asks that the fleece alone be dry and all the ground dewy; God does so that night, with those two conditions expressly repeated.

relationship: Same-chapter second night's conditions repeat the requested reversal
rationale: The dry fleece and dewy ground are the precise reversal Gideon requested for the second test, distinguishing it from the first wet-fleece sign.

relationship: Gathered forces after Gideon's tribal summons
rationale: The men answering Gideon's messengers form the preceding gathering; the next scene places Gideon and his people in camp, with Midian and Amalek's camp north of him.

relationship: Warning against attributing deliverance or gain to one's own hand
rationale: The army is reduced lest Israel claim its own hand saved it; Deuteronomy likewise forbids attributing wealth to one's own strength and recalls the Lord as its giver.

relationship: Fearful men released under comparable battle instructions
rationale: Gideon is told to let the cowardly and afraid return; Deuteronomy likewise directs fearful, fainthearted men home, while the Judges account supplies its own numbers and Mount Gilead wording.

relationship: Same-chapter announced water test and the selected force
rationale: The Lord announces a further test at the water; the following verses distinguish drinking postures, number the lappers at three hundred, and choose them for deliverance.

relationship: Same-chapter drinking distinction, count and selection
rationale: The command separates tongue-lappers from those bending on their knees; the report counts three hundred lappers and the Lord selects that group for deliverance.

relationship: Same-chapter counted three hundred and their appointed role
rationale: The three hundred tongue-lappers are expressly the men by whom the Lord promises to save Israel and deliver Midian, while the other people are dismissed.

relationship: Same-chapter promised deliverance by three hundred and divine battlefield action
rationale: The Lord promises deliverance through the three hundred; the attack report again numbers three hundred trumpets and attributes the camp's swords turning against neighbours to the Lord.

relationship: Same-chapter retained force and its subsequently distributed equipment
rationale: Gideon retains three hundred with provisions and trumpets; he later divides the three hundred into three companies and adds jars with torches to their trumpet equipment.

relationship: Same-chapter nighttime assurance confirmed through the heard dream
rationale: The Lord tells Gideon He has delivered the camp; the enemy's interpreted dream repeats that delivery, and Gideon returns to announce it to Israel.

relationship: Same-chapter conditional accompaniment and the actual descent with Purah
rationale: The Lord permits Gideon to take Purah if he fears going down; the following instruction explains listening for encouragement and records their going down together.

relationship: Same-chapter instruction to listen and the strengthening message heard
rationale: The Lord directs Gideon to hear the camp's words; Gideon hears the dream and its interpretation, worships, and returns declaring the camp delivered into Israel's hands.

relationship: Repeated locust multitude and innumerable-camel description
rationale: The enemy camp's locust comparison and camels beyond numbering repeat the earlier portrayal of the invaders entering Israel's land with tents and livestock to ruin it.

relationship: Same-chapter barley-cake dream and its expressed interpretation
rationale: The dream's tumbling barley cake overturns Midian's tent; the hearer explicitly interprets it as Gideon's sword and the Lord delivering Midian and the camp.

relationship: Same-chapter interpretation heard and Gideon's responsive proclamation
rationale: The interpretation says the Lord has given Midian to Gideon; after hearing it, Gideon worships and tells Israel the Lord has given them Midian's camp.

relationship: Same-chapter worship and confidence prompted by the enemy's dream
rationale: Gideon's worship and announcement follow his hearing the barley-cake dream and its interpretation as the Lord's delivery of Midian to him.

relationship: Same-chapter three-company equipment plan and its performance
rationale: The three companies receive trumpets and jars containing torches; the attack describes jars shattered, trumpets sounded and torches held, with Gideon's hundred beginning the action.

relationship: Same-chapter instruction to imitate Gideon and the companies' response
rationale: Gideon tells the men to copy his actions; he and his hundred break jars and sound trumpets, followed by the matching actions of all three companies.

relationship: Same-chapter commanded acclamation and its reported expanded form
rationale: The command calls for trumpets and the cry For the Lord and for Gideon; the execution adds A sword to that acclamation while sounding the trumpets.

relationship: Same-chapter Gideon's opening attack uses the assigned equipment
rationale: Gideon's hundred sound trumpets and smash jars at the middle watch, carrying out the earlier three-company plan that assigned trumpets and torch-containing jars.

relationship: Same-chapter companies repeat the signal and cry after Gideon's opening
rationale: All three companies sound trumpets and break jars after Gideon's initial action; their cry follows the commanded Lord-and-Gideon formula with an added sword expression.

relationship: Same-chapter Israel's surrounding stance and the enemy camp's flight
rationale: The men stand around the camp while it runs and flees; the next report attributes swords against neighbours to the Lord and specifies the fleeing camp's route.

relationship: Neighbour-directed swords amid enemy battle confusion
rationale: The Lord turns the camp's swords against neighbours in Gideon's battle; Saul's battle account likewise reports each man's sword against his neighbour amid great confusion.

relationship: Same-chapter divine action answers the promise concerning three hundred
rationale: The Lord's action amid three hundred sounding trumpets realizes the earlier promise to save by the three hundred lappers and deliver Midian into Israel's hand.

relationship: Named tribes responding and later pursuing Midian
rationale: Naphtali, Asher and Manasseh pursue Midian after those tribes were summoned; the earlier summons also includes Zebulun, which the pursuit notice does not name.

relationship: Control of Jordan access during pursuit
rationale: Gideon commands Ephraim to seize the waters as far as Beth-barah and the Jordan; Ehud's force specifically seizes Moab's Jordan crossings and blocks passage.

relationship: Captured Midianite rulers and Gideon's acknowledgment of Ephraim
rationale: The capture and killing of Oreb and Zeeb precede Gideon's statement that the Lord gave those two rulers into Ephraim's hand, calming their dispute.

relationship: Ephraim's complaint at not being called to battle
rationale: Ephraim disputes with Gideon for not calling it against Midian; it later makes the same complaint to Jephthah about Ammon, adding a threat to burn his house.

relationship: Same-chapter harvest comparison explained by Ephraim's capture
rationale: Gideon's comparison of Ephraim's gleanings with Abiezer's vintage is followed by his naming Ephraim's capture of Oreb and Zeeb as greater than his own achievement.

relationship: A conciliatory answer turning away anger
rationale: Ephraim's spirit relaxes after Gideon's answer credits its achievement; Proverbs describes a yielding answer turning away wrath, illustrating the effect of his response.

relationship: The retained three hundred continue across Jordan
rationale: The three hundred crossing with Gideon, hungry and fainthearted, are the number earlier selected for deliverance and retained after the other men were sent home.

relationship: Same-chapter bread request and the rulers' refusal
rationale: Gideon requests bread for hungry men pursuing Zebah and Zalmunna; Succoth's rulers question whether those kings are already captured and withhold aid.

relationship: Same-chapter Succoth's taunt repeated after the kings' capture
rationale: The rulers refuse bread by questioning possession of Zebah and Zalmunna; Gideon later presents those kings and recalls the taunt in his confrontation with Succoth.

relationship: Same-chapter threatened wilderness-thorn punishment carried out
rationale: Gideon threatens to tear Succoth's flesh with wilderness thorns when the kings are delivered; after capture he uses wilderness thorns against its rulers and elders.

relationship: Same-chapter Penuel's matching refusal and its later punishment
rationale: Penuel answers Gideon as Succoth had answered; his later return brings demolition of Penuel's tower and killing of its men, following the intervening warning.

relationship: Same-chapter tower-demolition threat and its performance
rationale: Gideon promises to demolish Penuel's tower when he returns in peace; the later notice explicitly reports that demolition and also the city's men being killed.

relationship: Same-chapter remaining camp and the capture of its named kings
rationale: The surviving camp is introduced with Zebah and Zalmunna and its own numbers; the following victory notice captures both named kings and overthrows their camp.

relationship: Same-chapter attack on a confident camp and the kings' flight
rationale: Gideon's strike catches the camp while confident; Zebah and Zalmunna then flee, are pursued and captured, and their camp is wiped out.

relationship: Same-chapter pursued kings are finally captured
rationale: The capture of Zebah and Zalmunna completes the pursuit Gideon had named when requesting food for his hungry men at Succoth.

relationship: Same-chapter return from battle and confrontation at Succoth
rationale: The return by the ascent of Ares introduces the seizure of a Succoth informant, Gideon's confrontation over refused bread, and punishment of the city's rulers and elders.

relationship: Same-chapter recorded rulers and elders become the objects of punishment
rationale: The captured young man records Succoth's rulers and elders, seventy-seven men; Gideon subsequently takes the city's rulers and elders and punishes them with wilderness thorns.

relationship: Same-chapter captured kings answer the earlier refusal of bread
rationale: Gideon presents Zebah and Zalmunna and recalls the rulers' question about having their hand already in his hand, reversing the premise of Succoth's refusal.

relationship: Same-chapter thorn punishment answers Gideon's declared threat
rationale: The punishment of Succoth's rulers and elders with wilderness thorns follows Gideon's prior promise to use wilderness thorns when the Lord delivered the kings to him.

relationship: Same-chapter destruction of Penuel's tower fulfills the warning
rationale: Penuel's tower is demolished as Gideon had threatened after its refusal, while the execution notice additionally states that he killed the city's men.

relationship: Same-chapter the Tabor victims identified as Gideon's brothers
rationale: Gideon questions Zebah and Zalmunna about those killed at Tabor; his next statement identifies the victims as his mother's sons and makes their deaths grounds for not sparing the kings.

relationship: Same-chapter family killings and Gideon's execution of the kings
rationale: Gideon says he would have spared the kings had they kept his brothers alive; he later personally kills Zebah and Zalmunna after their appeal for him to act.

relationship: Same-chapter fearful firstborn and Gideon's ensuing action
rationale: Jether does not draw his sword because he is young and afraid; the kings then call for Gideon himself, and he rises and kills them.

relationship: Same-chapter the kings' appeal follows the boy's refusal
rationale: The kings ask Gideon himself to strike them, after his firstborn Jether had not drawn his sword because of youth and fear, distinguishing the two actors.

relationship: Israel requesting a human ruler in different circumstances
rationale: Israel asks Gideon and his sons to rule because of rescue from Midian; the later request to Samuel asks for a king to judge them like the other nations.

relationship: The Lord's kingship acknowledged and later rejected
rationale: Gideon declines rule for himself and his son, affirming the Lord's rule; the Lord later interprets Israel's demand for a king as treating His own reign as nothing.

relationship: Gold earrings requested before a religious object is fashioned
rationale: Gideon requests earrings from spoils; Aaron requests earrings from wives and daughters and fashions a calf, distinguishing the sources and the later objects rather than equating them.

relationship: Same-chapter earring donations and their stated weight
rationale: The people agree and throw gold earrings onto Gideon's cloak; the next notice gives the requested earrings' weight as seventeen hundred shekels apart from other listed trophies.

relationship: Same-chapter collected gold and the ephod subsequently made
rationale: The earring gold is weighed separately from other trophies; the next report says Gideon made it into an ephod, after which Israel followed it and it became a household stumbling block.

relationship: Collected gold made into a religious object
rationale: Gideon's collected gold becomes an ephod that Israel follows and that becomes a stumbling block to Gideon and his household; Aaron likewise receives donated gold and makes a calf, preserving the distinct objects.

relationship: Midian's defeat reverses its earlier domination
rationale: The forty-year quiet after Midian's humiliation contrasts with the opening notice that Israel was handed to Midian for seven years, preserving both stated periods.

relationship: Explicit identity connecting Jerubbaal and Gideon
rationale: The return notice names Jerubbaal son of Joash; the earlier camp introduction expressly identifies Jerubbaal as Gideon, linking that name with the campaign's leader.

relationship: Seventy sons and the later fratricide notice
rationale: Gideon's seventy sons introduce the family struck by Abimelech; the later account retains seventy killed on one stone and Jotham's escape without recalculating the number.

relationship: Abimelech's maternal connection with Shechem
rationale: The concubine at Shechem bears Abimelech; his next chapter opens with Abimelech seeking his mother's brothers and kindred there, making that maternal connection politically significant.

relationship: Differing descriptions of Abimelech's mother in narrative and accusation
rationale: The narrator describes Gideon's concubine at Shechem bearing Abimelech; Jotham's accusation calls Abimelech the son of his father's slave girl, preserving both supplied descriptions.

relationship: Same-chapter Gideon's death and the explicitly ensuing religious relapse
rationale: The death and burial notice is followed by a statement that, when Gideon died, Israel returned to the Baalim and made Baal-berith its god.

relationship: Religious relapse after the judge's death
rationale: Israel's return to the Baalim after Gideon's death exemplifies the book's earlier description of people turning back to other gods when a judge dies.

relationship: Forgotten rescue corresponds to the prophet's earlier recollection
rationale: Israel forgets the Lord who rescued it from surrounding enemies; the prophet had expressly recalled rescue from Egypt and all oppressors and the gift of their land.

relationship: Unrequited kindness to Gideon's house and Jotham's accusation
rationale: The notice says Gideon's house received no mercy despite his goodness; Jotham later contrasts his father's dangerous rescue of Israel with the killing of his sons.

relationship: Abimelech's birth at Shechem and his maternal alliance there
rationale: Abimelech approaches his mother's kin at Shechem after the earlier birth notice places Gideon's concubine there and names the son she bore Abimelech.

relationship: Same-chapter appeal to kinship and its stated persuasive effect
rationale: Abimelech asks his maternal relatives to invoke his flesh-and-bone kinship; Shechem's men incline toward him specifically because they say he is their brother.

relationship: Same-chapter Shechem's preference and Abimelech's enthronement
rationale: Shechem's men favor Abimelech because of kinship; those men later gather with the house of Maallon and make him king at Shechem.

relationship: Same-chapter Baal-of-the-Covenant house as source of silver and later refuge
rationale: Silver from the house of Baal of the Covenant is used to hire Abimelech's followers; later Shechem's Tower men seek refuge in the stronghold of the house bearing that name.

relationship: Same-chapter fratricide and the stated purpose of ensuing judgment
rationale: Abimelech kills his brothers on one stone while Jotham hides; the later explanation says their blood is laid upon Abimelech and the Shechem men who enabled him.

relationship: Abimelech's kingship reverses Gideon's refusal of family rule
rationale: Shechem makes Abimelech king after his father Gideon had refused rule for himself and his son and affirmed that the Lord would rule Israel.

relationship: Same-chapter Jotham's public address and the stated application
rationale: Jotham calls Shechem to listen from Mount Gerizim; after the tree fable he applies its warning to their treatment of Jerubbaal's house and choice of Abimelech.

relationship: Same-chapter olive-tree kingship offer and refusal
rationale: The trees ask the olive to reign; it refuses to leave its richness, which God and human beings glorified, for rule over the trees.

relationship: Same-chapter productive trees' parallel refusals
rationale: The olive refuses to leave its richness for rule; the fig likewise values sweetness and produce, and the vine its wine as human gladness from God.

relationship: Same-chapter fig-tree kingship offer and refusal
rationale: The invitation to the fig tree is answered by its refusal to abandon sweetness and good produce in order to rule the trees.

relationship: Same-chapter fig and olive retain their produce instead of ruling
rationale: The fig's refusal to leave sweetness and good produce repeats the olive's refusal to leave its richness, with each contrasting its productive role and proposed kingship.

relationship: Same-chapter vine kingship offer and refusal
rationale: The trees' request that the vine reign is answered by its refusal to leave wine, described as human beings' gladness from God, to rule trees.

relationship: Same-chapter vine and olive refuse abandonment of their valued produce
rationale: The vine values wine as human gladness from God; the olive values its richness glorified by God and people, and both refuse to leave their produce for rule.

relationship: Same-chapter bramble invitation and conditional acceptance
rationale: The bramble receives the same call to reign, but answers with conditional shelter and a threat of fire, differing from the productive trees' refusals.

relationship: Same-chapter fable's conditional fire and its stated application
rationale: The bramble threatens fire if its kingship is not sincere; Jotham then speaks conditional fire from Abimelech against Shechem and from Shechem against Abimelech.

relationship: Royal political fables using a low thorn plant and Lebanon's cedar
rationale: Jotham's bramble threatens Lebanon's cedars; Joash's thornbush asks a Lebanon cedar for marriage and is trampled, using similar plant imagery in a different royal warning.

relationship: Jotham's test of treatment and the narrator's ingratitude notice
rationale: Jotham asks whether Shechem dealt well with Jerubbaal and his house according to his deeds; the preceding narrator already says that house received no mercy for Gideon's goodness.

relationship: Jotham recalls his father's perilous rescue from Midian
rationale: Jotham says his father risked his life to rescue Israel from Midian; the night attack recounts Gideon's company entering the camp and the Lord overturning the enemy force.

relationship: Same-chapter accusation repeats the narrated killing of brothers
rationale: Jotham accuses Shechem of killing his father's seventy sons on one stone; the earlier narrative records Abimelech's deed and the youngest brother's escape.

relationship: Same-chapter conditional mutual joy rests on the earlier stated test
rationale: Jotham's blessing of mutual joy with Abimelech depends on truth and integrity toward Jerubbaal's house, repeating the criterion introduced before his charge of wrongdoing.

relationship: Same-chapter threatened fire and Shechem's later destruction by fire
rationale: Jotham threatens fire from Abimelech consuming Shechem's men; Abimelech's followers later burn the stronghold over Shechem's Tower inhabitants, killing about a thousand men and women.

relationship: Same-chapter the surviving youngest brother escapes Abimelech again
rationale: Jotham initially survives the brothers' killing by hiding; after his address he flees to Rara because of his brother Abimelech, preserving the supplied place-name.

relationship: Same-chapter royal installation and the stated period of rule
rationale: Shechem's making Abimelech king is followed by the summary that he ruled over Israel for three years, distinguishing the local installation from the stated scope of rule.

relationship: Same-chapter God-sent rupture and its stated blood-guilt purpose
rationale: God sends an evil spirit and Shechem breaks faith with Abimelech; the following explanation connects this rupture with returning the slain brothers' blood upon killer and supporters.

relationship: Same-chapter announced recompense and the narrator's final verdict
rationale: The explanation assigns the brothers' blood to Abimelech and his Shechem supporters; the closing notices expressly attribute both parties' recompense to God.

relationship: Same-chapter mountain ambushes express the announced breach of loyalty
rationale: Shechem's road ambushes against Abimelech and its plundering follow the narrator's statement that the city's men acted faithlessly toward his house after the God-sent rupture.

relationship: Same-chapter trusted newcomer voices a challenge to Abimelech
rationale: Shechem trusts Gaal and his brothers; Gaal subsequently questions service to Abimelech and offers to remove him if the people are put in his hand.

relationship: Same-chapter festival cursing develops into an explicit political challenge
rationale: The vineyard celebration in their god's house includes curses against Abimelech; Gaal's following speech challenges Abimelech's authority and proposes his removal.

relationship: Repeated name and parental description of Hamor and Shechem
rationale: Gaal's speech names Hamor as Shechem's father; Genesis uses that same name and parental description in Jacob's field purchase, without supplying a new genealogy for Gaal's audience.

relationship: Same-chapter Gaal's challenge and Zebul's demand that he fight
rationale: Gaal boasts he would remove Abimelech and would challenge him to increase his army; Zebul later confronts his disparagement and tells him to go out and fight.

relationship: Same-chapter Zebul's anger and the message it prompts
rationale: Zebul becomes furious at Gaal's words, then sends Abimelech a report about Gaal and his brothers with gifts, preserving the message's actual description.

relationship: Same-chapter reported arrival and the narrator's preceding account
rationale: Zebul reports that Gaal and his brothers have arrived, matching their earlier narrated arrival, while his message additionally portrays them as besieging the city against Abimelech.

relationship: Same-chapter proposed nighttime ambush and its execution
rationale: Zebul urges Abimelech and his men to rise by night and ambush in the field; Abimelech rises by night and lays ambush against Shechem in four companies.

relationship: Same-chapter proposed morning encounter and the ensuing confrontation
rationale: Zebul anticipates an advance at sunrise and Gaal's coming out; morning brings Gaal at the gate, troops rising from ambush, and finally his going out to fight.

relationship: Same-chapter nighttime deployment follows Zebul's proposed plan
rationale: Abimelech's nocturnal ambush in four companies follows Zebul's instructions to rise at night and prepare for a morning attack, retaining the narrated company count.

relationship: Same-chapter emerging ambushers and Gaal's first report of them
rationale: The narrator identifies Abimelech's men rising from ambush; Gaal then reports people descending the mountains, while Zebul initially calls what he sees shadows.

relationship: Same-chapter first sighting disputed and the subsequent confrontation
rationale: Zebul initially calls Gaal's sighting mountain shadows; Gaal repeats his report from specified routes, and Zebul then challenges him to fight the people he had disparaged.

relationship: Same-chapter repeated troop sighting leads to the challenge to fight
rationale: Gaal reports approaches by the Navel of the Land and Watchers' Oak; Zebul responds with a challenge, after which Gaal goes out to fight Abimelech.

relationship: Same-chapter Zebul confronts Gaal's earlier boast
rationale: Zebul recalls Gaal's question about serving Abimelech and demands combat; the earlier speech had questioned that service and proposed removing Abimelech by force.

relationship: Same-chapter Gaal's battle and its outcome
rationale: Gaal goes out from before Shechem's men to fight Abimelech; the following account reports his flight before Abimelech and many slain near the city entrances.

relationship: Same-chapter pursuit and losses follow Gaal's decision to fight
rationale: Gaal's flight and the casualties near the city entrances are the reported outcome of his going out against Abimelech after Zebul's challenge.

relationship: Same-chapter Gaal's expulsion reverses his trusted arrival
rationale: Gaal and his brothers first arrive and gain Shechem's trust; Zebul later expels them so that they cannot dwell there, while Abimelech remains at Arima.

relationship: Same-chapter report of people in the plain prompts another ambush
rationale: Abimelech hears that people have gone into the plain; he then divides his force into three companies, watches their exit and attacks them from ambush.

relationship: Same-chapter three-company ambush develops into the city's fall
rationale: Abimelech's three-company ambush is followed by action at the gate and two companies attacking those in the field; the day's fighting ends in Shechem's capture and demolition.

relationship: Same-chapter gate and field attacks implement the renewed ambush
rationale: The gate position and the two companies' field attack belong to Abimelech's renewed operation, introduced by his division into three companies and watch upon the people leaving the city.

relationship: Same-chapter Shechem's destruction and the narrator's judgment notice
rationale: The city is captured, its people killed and its site demolished and salted; the closing notice attributes Shechem's returned wickedness and Jotham's fulfilled curse to God.

relationship: Same-chapter refuge in the stronghold and its disastrous outcome
rationale: Shechem's Tower men enter Baal-of-the-Covenant's stronghold; the later burning kills its inhabitants, described as about a thousand men and women rather than only the earlier named men.

relationship: Same-chapter report of the gathering prompts the wood-and-fire assault
rationale: After hearing the Tower men have gathered, Abimelech leads wood-cutting on Mount Zalmon, and his followers carry out the burning of the occupied stronghold.

relationship: Same-chapter Abimelech's model action and its imitation
rationale: Abimelech cuts and shoulders wood, commanding imitation; each follower then cuts a load, carries it and helps burn the stronghold over the people inside.

relationship: Same-chapter literal fire corresponds to Jotham's warning about Shechem
rationale: Abimelech's followers burn Shechem's Tower stronghold over its inhabitants, giving a literal narrative expression to Jotham's threatened fire from Abimelech consuming Shechem's men.

relationship: Same-chapter Thebez's capture followed by the decisive tower encounter
rationale: The attack on Thebez leads into its inhabitants' refuge on the tower, Abimelech's attempted burning, the woman's millstone throw and his armour-bearer's final blow.

relationship: Same-chapter two populations taking refuge in strongholds
rationale: Thebez's men, women and leaders shelter on a fortified tower; Shechem's Tower people had sheltered in a stronghold that Abimelech's followers burned, distinguishing the locations and outcomes.

relationship: Same-chapter repeated fire tactic at a different fortified refuge
rationale: Abimelech approaches Thebez's tower to burn it after successfully burning Shechem's stronghold with carried wood; the Thebez passage describes an attempt, not a completed burning.

relationship: Explicit later recollection of Abimelech and the woman's millstone
rationale: Both name Abimelech as struck by a woman's millstone fragment; Samuel names his father Jerubbaal and calls the death-place Thamasi, while Judges' surrounding narrative names Thebez.

relationship: Same-chapter crushed skull and the request to control the manner of death
rationale: The woman's millstone crushes Abimelech's skull; he then asks his armour-bearer to kill him to avoid the saying that a woman killed him, and the servant pierces him.

relationship: Wounded rulers requesting death from their armour-bearers
rationale: Abimelech's armour-bearer obeys his request to avoid a woman's credit for his death; Saul's armour-bearer refuses his request to avoid enemy piercing and mockery, and Saul falls on his sword.

relationship: Same-chapter the ruler's death and his men's dispersal
rationale: The armour-bearer pierces Abimelech and he dies; Israel's men see that he is dead and each goes to his place, directly connecting death and dispersal.

relationship: Same-chapter final divine recompense fulfills the stated blood-guilt purpose
rationale: The final notice says God returned Abimelech's wrong against his father through the brothers' killing; the earlier explanation had assigned those brothers' blood to him and his supporters.

relationship: Same-chapter narrator explicitly connects Shechem's judgment with Jotham's curse
rationale: The narrator says Jotham's curse came upon Shechem's men, connecting their judgment with the earlier conditional words of destructive fire between Abimelech and Shechem.

relationship: Same-chapter Tola's introduction, judging period and burial
rationale: Tola is introduced as Israel's rescuer dwelling in Samaria; the next notice gives his twenty-three years of judging and burial in that same named place.

relationship: Same-chapter Tola's burial notice completes his introduced biography
rationale: The twenty-three-year judging and burial in Samaria conclude the introduction of Tola son of Puah, who dwelt in Samaria in Ephraim's hill country.

relationship: Same-chapter Jair's judging period and subsequent burial
rationale: Jair the Gileadite is introduced as judging twenty-two years; the later notice records Jair's death and burial in Rammo, without identifying him with earlier men named Jair.

relationship: Judge-family notices counting descendants and their donkey mounts
rationale: Jair has thirty-two sons riding thirty-two young donkeys and holding thirty-two cities; the later notice gives forty sons and thirty grandsons riding seventy donkeys, preserving the distinct counts.

relationship: Same-chapter Jair's death closes the notice of his judgeship
rationale: The death and burial of Jair follow his introduction as the Gileadite judge of twenty-two years, retaining Rammo as the supplied burial name.

relationship: Renewed service of other gods after the judges' period
rationale: Israel again serves the Baalim and named neighbours' gods, abandoning the Lord; the book's earlier pattern likewise describes renewed other-god service when a judge dies.

relationship: Repeated anger and sale into enemies' hands
rationale: Both describe the Lord's anger against Israel and His selling or delivering it into enemies' hands; chapter10 specifically names the foreigners and the sons of Ammon.

relationship: Oppression in Gilead and the later search for a deliverer
rationale: The eighteen-year oppression concerns Israel in Gilead; the continuing Ammonite fighting later prompts Gilead's elders to seek Jephthah from Tob.

relationship: Same-chapter Ammonite pressure and the opposing camps
rationale: Ammon crosses Jordan against Judah, Benjamin and Ephraim, producing distress; the later camp notice describes further military preparation, placing Ammon in Gilead and Israel at Mizpah.

relationship: Corporate confessions of sin before the Lord
rationale: Israel confesses sin through forsaking God and serving the Baalim; the gathering at Mizpah likewise confesses sin before the Lord, with its own fasting and water-pouring setting.

relationship: An expressly named earlier oppressor and the recorded rescue
rationale: Egypt heads the Lord's recalled list of oppressors; Exodus gives the particular account of the Lord rescuing Israel from the Egyptians' hand at the sea.

relationship: Recollection of Midian and Amalek and the narrated deliverance
rationale: The Lord recalls rescue from Midian and Amalek among other oppressors; the earlier campaign names both in the camp and narrates the Lord turning its swords against neighbours.

relationship: Same-chapter rejected allegiance and the later removal of rival gods
rationale: The Lord refuses further rescue after Israel's other-god service; later Israel removes foreign gods and serves Him, while the source still reports His displeasure and weariness.

relationship: Challenge to chosen gods to provide rescue
rationale: The Lord tells Israel to seek rescue from its chosen gods; Deuteronomy similarly asks where the trusted gods are and calls them to arise as helpers and protectors.

relationship: Same-chapter repeated confession with a renewed urgent petition
rationale: Israel repeats its confession of sin, previously linked to Baalim service, now submitting to what pleases the Lord while urgently asking deliverance that day.

relationship: Foreign-god removal commanded and later enacted
rationale: Joshua commands removal of foreign gods and hearts directed to the Lord; Judges records their removal and worship of Him, while also retaining its stated divine displeasure and weariness.

relationship: Mizpah camp and the subsequent appointment there
rationale: Israel's camp is at Mizpah during the Ammonite crisis; Jephthah later speaks before the Lord at Mizpah after the elders appoint him head and leader.

relationship: Promised Gilead leadership and the ensuing agreement with Jephthah
rationale: Gilead's rulers promise headship to the man who begins fighting Ammon; the elders subsequently negotiate that role with Jephthah and appoint him head and leader.
